newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND - U.S. refiners to continue cutting costs.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - U.S. refiners to continue cutting costs.

text.p: U.S. refiners are likely next year to continue this year's torrid pace of restructurings, mergers and cost cutting in hopes of improving flagging profits and woeful returns on equity, oil analysts predict.

"The year 1996 represented major change. The restructuring and cost-cutting we saw was extensive. We've never seen anything like it and I think we'll see even more in 1997," said Fred Leuffer, oil analyst with Bear Stearns in New York.

"The refining business is a loser, with returns below the cost of capital, so every company is analyzing how to get margins up in their downstream operations," Leuffer said. "They're all considering divestitures, cost reductions and strategic allegiances" similar to those seen in 1996.
Jim Falvey, a senior Smith Barney energy analyst, said many refiners had "anemic" returns on capital of only three-to-four percent during the past six years.

"Among the independent refiners, Tosco Corp is the only exception," he added, referring to the Connecticut-based independent refiner that has enjoyed returns on capital of over 11 percent between 1993 and 1995.
"It's a very competitive business and there is a global surplus of refining," Falvey said, noting this is one factor that has kept margins at most refineries at paltry levels.

Overall, U.S. margins on refined products hovered near $3.78 a barrel for much of 1996, according to Salomon Brothers analyst Paul Ting -- not far above the average break-even point for U.S. refineries of between $2.75 and $3.00, Ting said.
Leuffer said refining margins should be helped in 1997 by an expected $2.50-to-$5.00-per-barrel drop in the cost of crude oil and continued cutbacks by refineries on overall expenditures.

"Refinery expenditures have come down 25 percent in 1996 and I think they will be flat in 1997," he said, adding most refineries have now completed expensive plant upgrades required to make cleaner-burning fuels such as reformulated gasoline.
And he said a likely two percent increase in U.S. demand for refined products in 1997 should also help margins improve.
But he and Falvey agreed continued cost cutting will be required to give margins a rosier glow of health.
Among this year's milestones, they noted:

* Texaco Inc and Shell Oil Co. confirmed in October they were discussing a combination of their U.S. downstream assets, as well as those of Star Enterprise, Texaco's joint venture with state-owned Saudi Aramco.

The three-way combination would likely lead to cost savings of over $1 billion, according to some industry observers, and bring together Shell's more than 8,700 branded retail outlets with Texaco/Star's 14,000 for a 15 percent share of the market. Texaco said it expected to sign a letter of intent on the deal in the 1997 first quarter.

* Tosco's $25 million bargain-basement purchase in February of British Petroleum's 185,000 barrel-per-day (bpd) refinery in Marcus Hook, Pennsylvania. After wringing substantial cost savings from labor union workers, Tosco agreed to spend $50 million to upgrade the mothballed plant and reopen it next summer.

* Tosco's agreement in November to pay $1.4 billion to acquire the fixed assets of Unocal Corp's 76 Products Co, including three refineries in California and 1,350 retail sites on the West Coast and in Hawaii.

Analysts said the deal would allow Unocal to save up to $250 million in capital expenditures on California downstream operations -- which it would presumably redirect to international exploration and production.

And Tosco said choreographing Unocal's assets with Tosco's two profitable refineries in Avon, California, and Ferndale, Washington, would produce substantial selling, general and administrative cost savings.

* Ashland Inc's announcement on Dec 9 that it would restructure its core units to improve profitablility. Although the company did not specify cost-cutting targets or timetables, analysts widely expect Ashland to sell its exploration unit -- valued by Leuffer at up to $450 million.

* Valero Energy Corp's decision in November to spin off its refining assets into a separate company and merge its natural gas assets with an existing operator. Valero said the restructuring should cut outstanding debt to around $375 million from current levels of about $925 million.

* On Dec 3, stockholders approved the $850 million swap-stock merger of Diamond Shamrock DRM.N and Ultramar Corp ULR.N into a new firm called Ultramar Diamond Shamrock Corp, to be based in San Antonio, Texas.
Some analysts described it as a defensive merger, designed mainly to prevent either of the companies from being gobbled up by larger competitors. Others have questioned the fit,
noting that Diamond Shamrock's turf was Texas and Southwest, whereas Ultramar's refining and marketing strongholds were in California and Eastern Canada.

* Sun Co Inc said on Dec 4 it would cut more than 200 jobs, or 20 percent of the workforce, at its 175,000 bpd refinery in Marcus, Hook, Pennsylvania. And in another cost-cutting move, the struggling independent said it would also eliminate 75 jobs at its refinery in Yabucoa, Puerto Rico.
-- ((New York Energy Desk, 212 859-1632))
